Wooden carved doors [8], masks [8], carved posts [6], wooden head on stand [1], wooden carved chair and stool  [2], wooden figures [2].

Album containing photographs and a journal by Capt. Herbert Sutherland Walker, relating to the British military campaign against the Kingdom of Benin in February 1897. The album contains seventy-seven photographic prints by Herbert Sutherland Walker (and/or others); and a handwritten diary by Walker, titled on the first page 'To BENIN & back', with entries dated from 16 January to 16 April 1897. Also in the album are newspaper cuttings, several published illustrations and photographs, and other printed matter. The album has been organised approximately chronologically by the compiler, though not exactly or consistently so, in order to show a narrative of the campaign ('Benin Punitive Expedition').
View of part of the British military campaign force's temporary base at Siri ['Ceri'], captioned in black ink below the print 'Reuter's Special [Service]'.
Portrait of a British officer, identified as Capt. Charles Ringer, standing, with washing hanging on a line behind him.

Group portrait of eight men, including British officers and others, standing and sitting – identified as Lieut. O'Shea (seated on ground), Maj. Frederick Landon (sitting, left), Capt. Charles Carter (sitting, centre), Capt. Herbert Walker (sitting, right), Capt. Charles Ringer (standing, left), Lieut. John Daniels (standing, second from left), Dr. Felix Roth (standing, second from right) and Capt. Searle (standing, right) – taken inside the king's (Oba's) residence, or palace or 'compound' area, in Benin City, in the aftermath of the British military attack on the city. Clearly visible at the left of the image are a number of commemorative heads and other figures, which were in the process of being collected and removed (elsewhere described in related documentation as 'loot').

Group portrait of nine men, standing, including six British officers or members of the Niger Coast Protectorate Force (N.C.P.F.) – identified as Maj. Norman Burrows (third from left), Dr. Robert Allman (fourth from left), Capt. Charles Ringer (fifth from left), Maj. Ernest Roupell (sixth from left), Alfred Turner (third from right) and Capt. Charles Carter (right) – and three unnamed African men (soldiers or auxiliaries/porters). They are pictured in front of the king's (Oba's) residence, or palace or 'compound', in Benin City.

Group portrait of eight men, including British officers and others, standing and sitting – identified as Maj. Frederick Landon (front row, left), Lieut.-Col. Bruce Hamilton (front row, centre), Lieut. John Daniels (front row, right), Capt. Charles Ringer (back row, left), Lieut. O'Shea (back row, second from left), Dr. Felix Roth (back row, centre), Capt. Herbert Walker (back row, second from right) and Capt. Charles Carter (back row, right) – taken inside the king's (Oba's) residence, or palace or 'compound' area, in Benin City, in the aftermath of the British military attack on the city. Clearly visible at the left of the image are a number of commemorative heads and other figures, which were in the process of being collected and removed (elsewhere described in related documentation as 'loot').

Three British officers – identified as Capt. Herbert Child, Ralph Moor (Commissioner and Consul-General of the Niger Coast Protectorate) and Alfred Turner – sitting and standing under cover at the edge of a building in Benin City. A caption below the print (written by the album's compiler) describes the building as 'Turner[']s compound', i.e. being the building where Turner had based himself.

View of a village in the bush or forest set on fire by British soldiers in order to destroy it. A handwritten caption elsewhere describes the photograph as showing '[t]he last of Amofia's village'. (Note that the caption below this print [1998.335.11], in Granville's album, appears therefore to be incorrect.)

Three Yoruba men using a branch as a pole to move the decaying or desiccated body (corpse) of a man or woman, described in the caption below the print (written by the album's compiler) as showing the men in the process of 'removing human sacrifice'.

View of the exterior wall of the king's (Oba's) residence, or palace or 'compound', in Benin City. A caption below the print (written by the album's compiler) describes this as being 'where the carriers were encamped', and indeed the group is just visible sitting together near the base of the wall, with several British officers nearby, as well as a large mounted gun (on wheeled carriage).

Group portrait of six British officers – identified as Reginald Granville, Capt. Henry Gallwey, James, A. Tucker, C. Dale and Hill – with native African porters standing and sitting behind them. Captions on either side of the print (written by the album's compiler) describe the scene as being a '[m]idday halt at Epbinni' while on the '[r]oad to Benin City'.

British troops with porters and auxiliaries disembarking and unloading supplies to establish the British military campaign force's initial (temporary) base at Siri ['Ceri'], captioned in black ink below the print 'At the base'.
